longForm.title: Assaye, 1803: The Battle Wellington Rated Higher Than Waterloo
longForm.excerpt: On 23 September 1803, Major General Arthur Wellesley crossed an unconfirmed ford, attacked a Maratha army seven times his strength, lost a third of his infantry, and won. He later said it was the finest thing he ever did.
paragraphs: The ground near the village of Assaye, at the confluence of the Kaitna and Juah rivers in the Deccan Plateau, did not favor an attack. No reverse slopes, no terrain for infantry to shelter behind, no complexity to exploit. Just flat scrub, two rivers, and a combined Maratha army of approximately 50,000 men with 100 cannon between them — guns that had been trained by European officers and were reliably served. Major General Arthur Wellesley arrived within striking distance on the morning of 23 September 1803 with approximately 7,000 effective troops: four battalions of British infantry, five battalions of Madras sepoys, and the 19th Light Dragoons with three regiments of Madras Native Cavalry. His second column, under Colonel Stevenson, was a full day's march away. The standard response in that situation is to wait. Wellesley attacked the same afternoon.

The reason he attacked came from a ford he had not yet confirmed. Wellesley's reconnaissance had established that the Kaitna River appeared impassable at the Maratha front. What it also established was that the villages of Peepulgaon and Assaye sat on opposite banks of the river, one north and one south. Wellesley's reasoning — that where two villages sit on opposite banks, there will be a crossing between them — is not a tactical principle you will find in any manual. It is the kind of spatial inference that either produces battlefield-grade intelligence or a column stuck chest-deep in an uncrossable river under fire. He sent a cavalry patrol. The ford existed. He crossed the entire force before the Maratha commanders could adjust their position to cover the new axis of advance. This single decision, made from terrain logic rather than confirmed reconnaissance, shaped everything that followed.

The Maratha army's gunners were competent. That point requires emphasis because British accounts of the Second Anglo-Maratha War have historically underplayed the quality of the opposition. The Maratha artillery arm had been reformed in the 1780s and 1790s under Benoit de Boigne, a Savoyard officer in Sindhia's service, and the competence de Boigne developed had survived his departure. When Wellesley's column appeared on their right flank after the Kaitna crossing, the Maratha commanders pivoted their line — swinging 100 guns to face the new threat while Wellesley's infantry was still deploying from march column into line of battle. The pivot was fast enough to bring substantial firepower to bear before the British infantry had fully formed. The British advance to contact was conducted under effective fire from the start.

The 74th Highland Regiment of Foot attacked toward the village of Assaye on the British right, where the gun concentration was heaviest. The 74th went into the attack with approximately 650 men. When the action at Assaye was over, roughly 450 of them were casualties — killed or wounded in a period that cannot have lasted much more than thirty minutes of close engagement. The regiment's commanding officer was wounded. Its formation broke. Wellesley rode into the collapse in person. His horse, Diomed, was shot and killed under him. A second horse was killed shortly afterward. He was wounded by a pike during the fighting in the Assaye perimeter. The scale of what happened to the 74th represents a command failure in the specific sense that the regiment was committed against the most heavily defended point without adequate support — though whether Wellesley had the infantry available to provide that support is a question the dispositions of the day do not clearly resolve.

The rest of the infantry action was as costly. The 78th Highlanders, advancing on the left toward the Maratha center, lost approximately 300 men. The Madras sepoy battalions sustained significant casualties throughout the line. By the point at which the Maratha infantry formations began to waver under the sustained pressure of the British advance — perhaps ninety minutes into the action — the British had committed the vast majority of their infantry and had insufficient reserves to consolidate any ground taken by the assault. The battle required a second instrument to finish it.

Colonel Patrick Maxwell held his cavalry — the 19th Light Dragoons and three Madras Native Cavalry regiments — through the infantry phase. He committed them when the Maratha line showed the first signs of coherent disorganization: gun crews leaving their pieces, infantry formations losing their dressing under fire, the pivot formation beginning to gap at its internal joints. Maxwell's charge went through the line, overran the artillery positions that had been doing the damage since the first moments of the engagement, and converted a costly infantry engagement into a rout. The pursuit was aggressive. Maxwell himself was killed during it, hit by fire from Maratha infantry that was still capable of organized resistance. The cavalry arm's effectiveness — held through the worst of the infantry fight, then committed at exactly the moment required — was the operational hinge on which the battle turned.

Total British and Indian casualties at Assaye were approximately 1,566 killed and wounded, from an effective infantry strength of roughly 4,500 engaged. A casualty rate of 35 percent in a single afternoon is not a number that appears in accounts of European battles without generating substantial controversy about command decisions. Wellesley reported the battle as a victory — which it was, in that the Maratha army was routed and 98 cannon captured. His private correspondence conveys something different: he described it, in letters written in the days that followed, as the most difficult action he had ever been engaged in. The 1,566 dead and wounded are the measure of what he meant.

Wellesley later told Samuel Rogers that he considered Assaye, not Waterloo, the finest thing he had ever done. The claim is worth taking seriously. Assaye required him to cross an unconfirmed ford, attack before his full force was assembled, sustain catastrophic infantry losses without breaking off the action — because breaking off across the Kaitna under fire was not a viable option once committed — and complete the battle with cavalry at the precise moment the infantry fight had made cavalry effective. All of those decisions were made in sequence under pressure, without the staff system and prepared positions that characterized his later campaigns. Waterloo required Wellesley to hold a position until the Prussians arrived. Assaye required him to generate a victory from a situation that, at several points in the afternoon, looked like disaster. The professional assessment in his private correspondence is consistent with what the operational record shows.

shortForm.title: Heartbreak Ridge, 1951: Fifty-Three Days for Ground the Armistice Gave Back
shortForm.excerpt: From August to October 1951, the US 2nd Infantry Division took Hill 931 in the Korean mountains, lost it, took it again, and lost it again — for fifty-three days. The armistice demarcation line, drawn in 1953, ran through the same ground.
paragraphs: Hill 931, the dominant peak in the ridge system overlooking the Mundung-ni Valley in central Korea, rises 931 meters above sea level approximately 20 kilometers northeast of Yanggu. In August 1951, armistice negotiations between UN and Communist commands had been running for six weeks without resolution on the question of the demarcation line. The principle was understood by both sides: the line would follow the positions held at the moment of ceasefire. That made every ridge in the negotiating zone an objective with political weight beyond its tactical value. The US 2nd Infantry Division received orders in late August to seize the Hill 931 ridge system — named Heartbreak Ridge by AP correspondent Hal Boyle before the battle was three weeks old. The division's commanders understood from the start they were being asked to take ground at costs that conventional tactical accounting could not justify.

The KPA 12th Division held prepared positions on 931 and the adjacent peaks — Hills 851 and 894 — organized specifically around the problem of air and artillery attack. The tunnel and bunker system allowed defenders to withdraw below ground during bombardment and reoccupy before attacking infantry could consolidate on the crest. This was not an improvised solution; it was a deliberate counter to UN air superiority that the Korean People's Army had been developing since 1950. The 2nd Division took Hill 931 in early September. They held it for hours before KPA counterattack drove them back. They took it again. They lost it again. The tactical sequence repeated without meaningful variation for fifty-three days because the physical problem — bunkers that survived bombardment, defenders who reappeared after the assaulting infantry passed — was not solved by any of the means applied. More artillery did not solve it. More infantry assaults did not solve it. What eventually solved it was ground-level negotiation: the KPA 12th Division was rotated out in mid-October and its replacement unit did not counterattack with the same intensity.

US 2nd Division casualties over the fifty-three-day battle totaled approximately 3,700 killed, wounded, and missing. The French and Dutch Battalions, attached throughout the operation, sustained additional losses not fully captured in divisional totals. Communist losses were estimated at 25,000–30,000 — a figure reflecting the sustained artillery and air bombardment applied to a force that held contested terrain at all costs. In conventional casualty exchange terms, Heartbreak Ridge was a tactical success: roughly one UN casualty for every seven Communist losses. That ratio did not change what happened in 1953. The armistice demarcation line was drawn through terrain that the 2nd Division had cleared in October 1951 and that the KPA had re-fortified by the time the ceasefire took effect. The men who died on 931 and its adjacent peaks died for a line that was subsequently set by negotiators. That is not a moral judgment about the battle. It is what the record shows.

onThisDay.headline: Japanese forces occupy Tulagi, triggering the Battle of the Coral Sea
onThisDay.summary: On 3 May 1942, Japanese naval forces landed at Tulagi in the Solomon Islands, establishing a seaplane base as part of Operation MO — the plan to capture Port Moresby and cut Australia's supply lines. The landing prompted US Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher to divert Task Force 17 for an immediate strike on the Tulagi anchorage, setting in motion the Battle of the Coral Sea (4–8 May 1942), the first naval battle in history fought entirely by carrier aircraft, with neither fleet's surface ships sighting the other.
